analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 158 to 164, Frozen Foods, Express et al. v. United States and Interstate Commerce Commission. Mr. Ghanay. May it please the Court, these cases arise out of Section 203B6 of the Interstate Commerce Act. That section is in Part 2 of the Interstate Commerce Act, which provides a comprehensive system of economic and safety regulation for interstate motor carriers. The section out of which these cases arise, Section 203B6, exempts from all economic regulations, that is, as to certificates of public convenience necessity, rates. And I quote, Now, while there are seven numbered appeals before the Court, they really amount to only two cases. Numbers 158 to 161 are referred to by the parties as the determination case. And it involves the single question of whether the decision of the Interstate Commerce Commission, in a proceeding entitled Determination of Exempted Agricultural Commodities, is reviewable by the courts. Numbers 162 to 164 are referred to by the parties as the complaint case. And it involves the single question of whether fresh and frozen dress poultry are exempt agricultural commodities under Section 203B6. I will make the sole argument for the appellants in numbers 159 and 160 in the determination case. And Mr. McDonald and I will divide the argument for appellants in the complaint case. I should state that appellant railroads have filed their own brief but are not participating in the oral argument. They're all in agreement on the first case, aren't they? Yes. There's nobody representing the district court besides the court. Nobody on this side of the table. Yeah. If I may discuss the determination case first, which involves the single question of whether the Commission's decision in that case is a reviewable order. Where is it? It begins in the record in number 158 at page 30. It runs from page 30 to page 102. Where is it possible to state what you mean the effective, the effect of any part of that order? For such and such expressions as in your view are a reviewable for man. I think it's concentrated in the findings beginning at the bottom. At the bottom of page 88. And running almost to the bottom of page 89. The paragraph beginning at the bottom of page 88. The Commission sets forth its general principle or test for determining whether a particular commodity is exempt or not exempt. And then the following full paragraph on page 89. It sets forth a long list of commodities which it has concluded are exempt as agricultural commodities. I should also add that in the course of the preceding discussion in its report, the Commission states at various places that in its judgment specific commodities such as just poultry are not exempt commodities. Where is that? At different portions of the preceding portion. The existing long paragraph on page 89. It says, It's a numerate. What are agricultural and set of commodities? And then at other... And in the discussion, you say there is an exclusion of what is not mentioned. Well, it's more specific than that. During the... At various points in the discussion, the Commission expressly states its conclusion that named commodities are not exempt. And there would be no trouble about it if they said, Accordingly, we shall regard parents who did our number of any other appropriate ending names applicable to the lives of the lives of the or frozen poultry as now. And parents have to be important. An appropriate character has to be obeyed or a lot of little parents. But they added nothing... No, no, no. They added no such directly operative language. Can you say that that's actually effective? Is that? Yes. Is there any doubt if they had 55,000 I think it would make the argument easier. Would there be any doubt about it? No. But a little later I shall like to point out that in its practical impact upon the transportation industry, the people in the industry had no doubt as to what the practical consequences were in terms of the need or lack of need for obtaining certificates of public convenience necessity or the need or lack of need for filing rate tariffs. Well, that might not be enough to name. But I told my disrespect to Chairman May at the conclusion of an argument saying that I would be willing to, I don't know, we're going to do this to that. That's what we get all over there. How is this order different from a sort of a letter that the Commissioner might have written to the industry saying this is the way we look at the matter? Is it really any different from that? Saying what it proposes to do? Well, as I should like to point out in more detail later on, we think that a distinguishing factor between what the Commission has done here and the huge mass of informal administrative determinations which everybody concedes are not and should not be reviewable, is that what the Commission did here was done after a formal hearing, the result of a formal proceeding. There is nothing formal, formally, formally, formally at the end of this. Anything on the record to the Commission except? No. No. We have to hear? Just this enumeration of commodities which the Commission had held to be exempt or not exempt, as the case may be. Where is the order on the basis of which the hearing was passed? Is that in your record? Yes, sir. It's at about page 29. Yes, on page 29. Page 29 of the record and number 158. And the order terminating it is the one at 101. Is it the discontinuing the proceeding? That is correct, sir. That's 968. Is that the proceeding? That's correct, sir. Have you a brief besides the one at 102? That's the brief filed on behalf of the United States and the Department of Justice. The two briefs filed on behalf of the Interstate Commerce Commission are printed with a blue cover. I'd like to go back. Certainly, sir. Yes. This part deals with explicit duties and obligations, right? Yes. This part, by this part, is meant part two, which is the whole system of regulation with respect to motor carriers. Requirements for certificates, filing of rates and tariffs. And the order on which, on the basis of the hearing was had, the version 2.0.3.6, is that in turn, is incorporated by reference to the whole system of regulation. Is that right? The hearing was had with reference to the meaning of these controlling words 2.0.3.6. Correct, sir. The 2.0.3.6, incorporated by reference to the law, the obligations and rights, the obligations of duties under the past and the past and the past. Well, Your Honor, I think I'd put it that 2.0.3.6 provides an exemption from all of the economic rights and duties under the Act. It all awaits to correct itself through obligations, which is the right to use of the law. It does indeed, sir. Now, the background of the determination can be summarized very briefly. What is now Part II originated as the Motor Carrier Act of 1935. And almost immediately after its enactment, there arose many questions as to what commodities were or were not exempted agricultural commodities. The issue arose as to many commodities. It arose in informal administrative determinations, informal commission decisions, and it was the subject of repeated litigation. The unhappy result was that 13 years later, in 1948, there was a good deal of confusion and uncertainty as to the scope of this important exemption. Now, in 1948, the Secretary of Agriculture and other persons had made fundamental objections to the Commission's holding in the so-called Harwood case that vegetables which had been washed, cleaned, and packaged were not exempt as agricultural commodities. Responding to those representations, the Commission reopened the Harwood case. In addition, by the order which appears on page 29 of this record, the Commission directed that an investigation, and I quote, be made into and concerning the meaning of the words agricultural commodity, not including manufactured products thereof. At the same time, the Commission directed that a hearing be held and a published notice of the hearing in the Federal Register. In brief, after 13 years of confusion and litigation and interpretation on a case-to-case and commodity-to-commodity basis, the Commission sought to arrive at an informed and consistent interpretation, applying Section 203b6 to agricultural commodities as a group. So early in 1948, late in 1948 and early in 1949, extensive hearings were held before a hearing examiner, who received voluminous evidence from representatives of the Department of Agriculture and many other interested parties. And after an examiner's report and oral argument before the full commission, the Commission in 1951 issued its decision in this determination proceeding. The report consists first of a detailed analysis of the legislative history of the agricultural exemption. And the Commission resorts extensively to accepted sources of interpretative material, dictionaries, decisions of the courts, particularly this court. And the Commission's report includes an extensive commodity-by-commodity discussion of the various processes and treatments which are applied to the different agricultural commodities. Now, the order at the end of the determination proceeding did not direct named persons to do or not to do anything. As set forth at page 101 of the record, it simply recites that full investigation of the matters and things involved has been made, and that the commission on the date hereof has made and filed its report on oral argument herein, containing its findings of fact and conclusions. And its order that the proceeding be made. And its order that the proceeding be in it hereby is discontinued. In 1954, frozen food express service. Before we get to that, may I ask this question, Mr. Jermaine, with the matter standing as it did when that order was made, what liabilities are frozen food subjected to? I suppose they don't pay attention to this order and go ahead and carry these commodities. What penalties is it subject to? It is subject to civil and criminal penalties. All right. How would the criminal penalties be invoked against it? Is it immediately subject to criminal penalties or must there first be some other proceeding before the board in the cease and desist order or something of that kind? Can the Interstate Commerce Commission, on the basis of this order alone, bring criminal prosecution against the frozen food? I don't think so. I think what the commission would do, at least what it has done in some cases, it has brought cease and desist proceedings, as it did in the companion frozen food case. And the violation of that cease and desist order would be the basis for a criminal proceeding. It could arise in another fashion, the commission could go into court in a civil proceeding for an injunction to enjoining continued violation of the Act. Could I ask you one question? Sorry, my sir. Does the commission usually publish its regulations and rules in the federal registry? The commission, when the commission issues rules, it ordinarily will set them up in the format of rules. They'll usually be entitled rules or regulations relating to such and such subject, like the trip leasing rules, which were before this court in the American Trucking Association's case. And it will publish them in the federal register, as required by the administrative procedure act. In this case, the commission did not publish in the federal register. Rather, it published its report in the determination case with its orders, in the printed volume of its orders. It seemed that, at least as regards the mechanics, the processing of the result of the proceeding, I would have to say that it treated it as an order rather than as rules in the conventional sense. When the cease and desist proceeding began, with which you referred to as the companion case here, how did they treat this order then? As an order, or did they go ahead and investigate further whether it should apply or not apply? The commission received additional evidence in this companion cease and desist proceeding. Although the evidence largely paralleled or duplicated the commission with the evidence which had been presented to the commission in the determination case. When you say they received the error. Oh, actually in that case it was a stipulation by the parties. By the parties? Yes. But that's very common even with reference to the same Paris, in the case of another shipper or another complainer or another landlord. Although there's a governing order as well to repeat new evidence for additional evidence. That's very common, isn't it? Yes, I believe it is. So this litigation over the determination case began in 1954 when Frozen Foods Express, which is a motor carrier, and the Secretary of Agriculture filed complaints in the District Court in Texas. Frozen Foods Express contended in its complaint that the commission had erred in classifying about 30 commodities as non-exempt. The complaint of the Secretary of Agriculture alleged that the commission had erred in classifying eight specified commodities as non-exempt. The United States, through the Department of Agriculture, supported the position of the Department of Agriculture. And various rail and motor carriers intervened in support of the commission's order. Now, the District Court, as your honors know, did not go into the merits and the correctness of the commission's decision in the determination case at all. It made just one holding that the commission's decision in the determination case was not a reviewable order. And in coming to that conclusion, the District Court relied primarily upon this Court's decision in the Los Angeles and Salt Lake Railroad case in 273 U.S., in which this Court held that an order of the commission placing a valuation upon railroad property was not subject to review. And the District Court seemed to rely heavily upon the classical language from the Los Angeles case, that the so-called order here complained of is one which does not command the carrier to do or to refrain from doing anything. Now, our position here is that the commission's determination in this case is distinguishable in its practical impact from the valuation order which was involved in the Los Angeles case. And thus distinguished, we think, it is reviewable under more recent developments in the law of review since the Los Angeles case. Now, comparing the practical impact of the two types of agency action, the valuation order in the Los Angeles case, as this Court pointed out, could have had no practical impact until there was a rate or some other kind of proceeding before the commission. And this Court noted specifically that, in the Los Angeles case, it is at least possible that no proceeding will ever be instituted, either before the commission or a court, in which the matters now complained of will be involved, or in which the errors alleged will be of legal significance. And similarly, the valuation order involved in that case did not leave any carrier even threatened with criminal penalties. By contrast, in the determination case, the commission's decision told motor carriers that they would be subject to criminal and civil enforcement proceedings if they carried commodities which the commission classified as non-exempt without obtaining appropriate certificates or permits of public convenience necessity. The total motor carriers, the total motor carriers, desiring to carry such certificates, that they must go to the expense and the inconvenience, and I regret to say a considerable period of time involved in obtaining appropriate certificates. So Mr. told us that you dragged the whole Part II behind this report, isn't that it? Much of Part II is involved, depending upon— Mr. It told him because that's the implication of the implementation of the Part II. That's right, sir. That's right, sir. This case isn't just this thing that you argued, and I probably—now, this is very important, isn't it, Mr. Genene, because I hope to remember your scrutiny— two more sentences would avoid intimidation. For another sentence, just want a few more words to spelling out what you argued in prison. And yet— That's what it's all about, isn't it? I think it could have been done. More care, a little more reason. But we do contend that the absence of a few formal sentences should not determine the issue of reviewability. That the practical impact is the same upon the person subject to regulation. I'm just suggesting that it's very important. With the passage of time through the years, it's become quite important. To the transport— It's a paragraph that we no doubt that it comes within Rochester and all the nations of Parliament. I know. We're all under pressure. We take for granted the thing. We don't pray we don't have to cut them out. One of the functions of the lawyers is to cut out because it's going to be able to change. And in support of what your Honor says, I think of the American broadcasting case last term. A slight difference in language apparently had the result that no one ever raised a question of reviewability. And we think the volume of actual litigation that has occurred since 1935 underlines sharply the practical impact of the Commission's determination of the scope of the agricultural commodity exemption. It's not a question of whether somebody may want to carry these commodities. Hundreds of people are already carrying, with or without certificates, the commodities involved in the Commission's determination of exempted agricultural commodities. And depending upon where a particular commodity is classified as exempt or not exempt, that has competitive consequences for those people. If a commodity is classified as exempt, that tells the people who are carrying it that they are subject to that, if they don't have certificates, they've got to obtain them or get out of the business. If a commodity is classified as exempt, it tells the carriers who handle that commodity that they are subject to unlimited unrestrained competition, both as to entry into the business and as to rates. Do you hear that what make one that keep more determined or isn't essential in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one place in one Now, it seems to us that such recent decisions of this Court as Columbia Broadcasting System of the United States and Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee v. McGrath stand for the proposition that it's the substance of administrative action and not the precise label that's placed upon it that determines whether it's reviewable. And it seems to us that those decisions also hold that under some circumstances persons may obtain review of agency action which isn't immediately addressed to them at all, which does not in terms require such persons to do or not to do anything. That is the practical impact of the order which determines reviewability. Now, we think the Act, the Interstate Commerce Act, clearly empowers the Commission to issue formal interpretations of such phrases as agricultural commodities, not including manufactured products thereof. Because Section 204 specifically provides that the Commission shall administer, execute, and enforce all provisions of this part. And empowers it to make all necessary orders in connection therewith and to prescribe rules, regulations, and procedure for such administration. In Federal Communications Commission, the American Broadcasting Company, in 347 U.S., this Court held that an almost identical grant of rulemaking power, almost verbatim, empowered the Federal Communications Commission to issue what were labeled as interpretative rules purporting to interpret a criminal lottery provision, a criminal code. And it was stated in these interpretative regulations of FCC that that Commission would use them as a guide in the exercise of its licensing powers, and particularly in the exercise of its power to review, to renew, or not to review, broadcast licenses. And in that case, the interpretative regulations, labeled as such, issued by the Communications Commission after a hearing, were reviewed by a three-judge district court and by this court, in a suit for an injunction without any actual attempt at enforcement of the regulations, either criminally or in actual licensing proceedings. And in any event, the case stands for the proposition, we believe, that the Interstate Commerce Commission, under a similar statutory provision, has been authorized by Congress to issue interpretations of the Act. Now, we don't think it should be decisive whether the Commission's decision in the interpretation case is labeled as a rule or as an order. But the significant thing is the practical impact upon the person subject to regulation. At the same time, I'd like to repeat that it is an important thing that a line be drawn between the mass of informal administrative interpretations and reviewable decisions or interpretations. We think that a line which fits here is the line drawn by Section 5D of the Administrative Procedure Act, which empowers administrative agencies, under certain conditions, to issue declaratory orders. We submit that the Commission's decision in the determination case. May it please the Court, at the recess, I had just started to call the Court's attention to the analogy, which we believe supports the reviewability of the determination, of declaratory orders under Section 5D of the Administrative Procedure Act. Section 5D, which is quoted in our brief at pages 28 and 29, provides that in every case of adjudication required by statute to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing, the agency is authorized in its sound discretion with like effect as in the case of other orders, the agency is authorized in its sound discretion with like effect as in the case of the Administrative Procedure Act. The Commission is a good order to issue a declaratory order to terminate a controversy or remove uncertainty. Page 28 of our brief. Yes, sir. Page 28 of the Commission's main brief. Starts at the bottom of page 28, continues at the top of page 29. Now, the Commission has the power and the duty to interpret and apply the agricultural commodity exemption in two types of cases of adjudication, within the meaning of the Procedure Act, in which a hearing is required. The first, cease and desist proceedings, and secondly, in determining applications for certificates of public convenience necessity. So, it seems to us that the scope and application of the agricultural commodity exemption, which the Commission is authorized by statute to determine after a hearing in two types of cases, is an issue which the Commission is empowered by Section 5D of the Procedure Act to determine in a declaratory order. And then assuming what Section 5D does not make too clear, but assuming that a declaratory order may be issued only after a hearing, well then in this case, the Commission held a hearing, an evidentiary hearing, before it issued, before it made its decision in the determination case. And the clear purpose of the determination after 13 years of uncertainty clearly was to terminate controversies and to remove uncertainties. The legislative history of Section 5D of the Procedure Act is quite sparse. It indicates only that it was generally modeled upon the Declaratory Judgments Act, and the report of the House Judiciary Committee does state specifically that such orders would be subject to judicial review as in the case of other orders. That's about the only light the legislative history of the Procedure Act throws on Section 5D. And we submit that the... You have in your own Act in Section 204 some authority to regulate the statute. Yes, that is a general grant of power to the Commission to issue orders and rules in the administration of the motor carrier provisions. Now, that's a general power. It doesn't specifically deal with the subject of declaratory orders. Whereas Section 5D, which is applicable to the Interstate Commerce Commission, as it is to other agencies, does deal specifically with the subject of declaratory orders. What did you do at American Truckers' administration? Those were... That was a rulemaking proceeding, labeled as such, and what emerged from that proceeding was in the form of rules and labeled rules. And that's the difference between rules there and what you do here? Yes. Here the Commission at no point said that it was issuing rules. And I have to state frankly that what the Commission did here was not in the format in which it usually would put rules of general applicability. And we do submit here that the fact that the Commission did not label what it did as a declaratory order is not conclusive. That if, in fact, it amounted to a declaratory order, and we think it did, then it should be reviewable just as much as though the Commission had said, this is a declaratory order issued under Section 5D. Now, the court below put a good deal of wing on the fact that the order which the Commission issued at the close of the determination proceeding was one discontinuing the proceeding. But as we point out in our brief, in the few cases in which the Commission has issued what it labeled as declaratory orders under Section 5D of the Administrative Procedure Act, it has used exactly the same technique at the end of the procedure. It has issued a report in which it issued the interpretation at which it had been requested, applying some provision of the statute to a particular set of facts. That appears in the Commission's report. And then in such declaratory order cases, the Commission issues an order, as it did here, saying, we've considered the matter, we've arrived at our conclusion, and the only ordering words are words which state that the proceeding is hereby discontinued. Is there any difference in the notice to parties or the parties who called upon to attend one of those hearings for a declaratory order or what was done here? In the two particular declaratory order cases I have in mind, they were requested by single individuals. Only one individual was involved in each of them. And here it was just a notice to the public, was it? Here it was a notice to the public because of its impact, possible impact upon, well, conservatively, many hundreds of carriers, and I would not know how many thousands of producers and shippers of agricultural commodities. A general public notice would be the only possible way of providing an opportunity for everyone with a legitimate interest to participate in the procedure. Here it was a notice published in the Federal Register. So in brief, our argument on the reviewability of the determination is that if interpretative rules issued after a hearing, as in the American Broadcasting case, or if an interpretation embodied in the form of a declaratory order is reviewable, as we think it is, then what the Commission did here, measured by its practical impact upon the person subject to regulation, is also reviewable. How would a trucker who was not in existence, a company who was not in existence at the time of this order, going into business, know whether the Commission had, A, made these rulings, or B, whether their order discontinued meant that they had abandoned them, how would he know all of them? Well, I think a reading of the determination as a whole would indicate to him that the order discontinued the proceeding was just a mechanical order which closed out the Commission's docket, leaving its interpretation of the statute standing. Well, at least it's been puzzled to the court and to lay trucking and to be puzzled no less possible. Well, the court had... It isn't reviewable, it isn't enforceable, I suppose. The court below was not left, as I read its decision, was not left with the thought that the Commission had gone through this long and expensive proceeding just for fun, or that it was abandoning the conclusions which it had arrived at. Why did it get to the court? It did, the Commission... It tells the motor carrier industry how the Commission will apply the exemption in the exercise of its licensing functions, and in the exercise of its enforcement powers. He can attack it, but in some situations he will do it at his own risk. Now, I think before the intermission, I may have misled the court to some extent. I believe I told the court that a criminal proceeding would lie only for violation of a cease and desist order. If I did state that, it was incorrect. A criminal enforcement proceeding will lie for violation of the act. So, you don't have to have a cease and desist order as the basis for a criminal proceeding. And there have been several prosecutions of carriers for carrying commodities which the Commission considered to be exempt, and which the carriers had gone ahead, and then had taken his chances by way of raising a defense in the criminal procedure. Now, the determination serves the purpose of warning everybody in the industry what the Commission's position will be, both in its licensing functions and in its enforcement policy. Under section 222-D. And, of course, he could raise, by way of defense, that the Commission's interpretation of the act was erroneous. But, of course, by that route, he has taken, he has to take the risk of criminal punishment. And he did proceed? We have, we have in several cases. There have been at least three successful criminal prosecutions with respect to just poultry alone, taking just one commodity. Now, I'd like to turn, if I may, to the companion case, the complaint case, which arose in somewhat different fashion. It arose when East Texas Motor Freight Lines and two other motor carriers complained to the Commission that frozen food products was transporting fresh and frozen meats and fresh and frozen dress poultry without an appropriate certificate of public convenience necessity. Therefore, the Commission held a hearing, and issued a report, an order, which held that those commodities were not exempt commodities, and directed frozen foods by order to cease and desist from carrying them without obtaining an appropriate certificate of public convenience necessity. I take it to the tarot, to the tarot, to the different tarot, to these fractions of fresh and for fresh and for dressed and for clothing. The rates would vary as to the commodity, and indeed they would vary between commodities. The rates, by and large, are those filed by the carrier. I understand that. I want to know specifically whether the rates are different, considerably different, and between live horses and dress horses and these horses. I do not know the answer. I'm sorry. Thereafter... I have to ask you one question before you leave the other question, Judge. Which parties are defending the judgment of the District Court insofar as the jurisdictional question is right? In the determination case? None of the parties are defending that. The government doesn't speak to this point, Judge. They do not speak to this point. I should say that the District Court raised that jurisdictional question, sua sponte, without it having been raised by any of the parties. So thereafter, frozen food and the Secretary of Agriculture certainly... If they will correct that in the case. I don't question that at all, sir. I agree with you. So thereafter, in the complaint case, frozen food and the Secretary of Agriculture brought suit, challenging the Commission's conclusion. The Commission had placed...well, I should say, the District Court sustained the Commission's conclusion as to fresh and frozen food. And frozen meats. And no appeal was taken from that aspect of the decision. The Commission...the District Court reversed the Commission as to fresh and frozen-dressed poultry. And that portion of the decision is here unappealed. Now, the Commission's decision to report in this complaint case as to fresh and frozen-dressed poultry was based upon, in part, upon its earlier decision with respect to poultry in the determination case, and in part upon evidence received in this companion complaint case. In its report in the determination case, the Commission reviewed the legislative history of Section 203 . Now, that exemption provision originated in the House Committee. And in its original form, it provided an exemption for motor vehicles used exclusively in carrying livestock or unprocessed agricultural products. Now, on the floor of the House, a question arose as to whether an exemption for unprocessed agricultural commodities would include such items as milk and cream. In response to that discussion, the chairman of the subcommittee in charge of the bill offered an amendment to delete the words unprocessed agricultural products and to substitute the present words agricultural commodities not including agricultural products thereof. And the chairman, in the chairman, in the chairman, in the chairman of the exception, indicated that it would cover pasteurized milk, gin, cotton, and cotton seed. Now, from this brief legislative history on the floor of the House, the Commission concluded that it was apparent that Congress intended the exemption to extend to commodities in the natural state and, to a limited extent, those further treated or processed. That is, the Commission sought to give full effect to that legislative history by recognizing that Congress did not intend that every type of processing or every type of treatment would be enough to take an agricultural commodity out of the exemption. But it felt that that legislative history was sufficiently sparse that it had to look to other indicia of meaning. So the Commission turned to dictionary definitions, and particularly to judicial decisions. And it gave particular weight to a decision of this Court in the Brogdex case, stating that manufacturing involves giving to materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations. All the parties concede that it's not enough just to look at the statute here, that the various meanings, the possible meanings of agriculture, manufacturing, particularly in borderline cases are such, that we're obligated to look for other indicia of meaning. Because that limited debate on the floor is all we have... The legislature, you have the flight on. You say, the fabulous, that's a fabulous, that's a fabulous, that's what we have to do the rest we can. Starting with the legislative history, what there is of. The word livestock can be studied. Yes. That's mentioned separately and in addition to agricultural commodities. Agricultural commodities and livestock. Livestock and agricultural commodities. The word livestock can be studied. Yes. It's not worth. Ordinary livestock. Ordinary livestock. And ordinary livestock is defined in another portion of the Act in such a way as it does not include poultry. It includes horses, goats, cattle, and so on. So poultry is not specifically mentioned in agriculture? That is correct, sir. Either as livestock or as agricultural commodities. It's not mentioned specifically any place. And you have to include that in agricultural commodities? That is correct, sir. No, we rely upon the analogy that after butchering and slaughtering, the products of butchering and slaughtering of livestock are meat. And we say that the net... And I understand meat is not an agricultural commodity. That is the commission's position which was sustained by the court below in this case. But a dead chicken, a lot of chicken, is...
